questions.a: If a program H could always decide halting, we could build a program that asks H about itself and does the opposite (loops if H says halt, halts if H says loop). That contradiction shows no such H can exist.

questions.q: What does 'undecidable' mean?
questions.a: No algorithm can always give a correct yes/no answer for every possible input.

days.guide: Time the student sorting a full deck alone; then split the deck among 2–3 helpers who each sort a part, then merge. Speedup = sequential time ÷ parallel time.

questions.q: Alone: 120 s. With two helpers (three people) the parallel time is 60 s. Speedup?
Why isn't the speedup 3 with three people?
questions.a: The merge step must be done sequentially and coordination takes time, limiting how much work runs in parallel.

days.guide: Give the Unit 5 test in the assessment key (about 40 minutes).

questions.q: What's the difference between parallel and distributed computing?
questions.a: Parallel computing splits a program into parts run simultaneously on multiple processors; distributed computing uses multiple separate computers connected over a network.

weeks.prep: Set up a Google account for Google Forms and Sheets. Recruit at least 15 respondents (family, co-op, friends). Preview Sheets 'Data → Data cleanup → Remove duplicates' and Find/Replace.
misconceptions: Survey questions with open text answers ('How much do you sleep?') produce messy data ('8', 'eight', '7-8 hrs'). Use consistent formats like numbers or multiple choice.
Deleting data that doesn't fit the hypothesis. Cleaning fixes errors and inconsistencies; it doesn't remove inconvenient real answers.
Collecting more personal info than needed. Ask only what the question requires; avoid names and addresses (privacy).
weeks.assessment_key: Cleaned dataset rubric (4 levels): 4 = consistent formats in every column, duplicates removed, invalid entries handled with a documented rule, at least 15 responses, and a reflection naming each cleaning decision and how it could affect conclusions (e.g. removing '20 hours of sleep' changes the average); 3 = clean data, thin reflection; 2 = some inconsistent entries remain; 1 = raw data.

days.guide: The student writes a question to investigate, then a 6-question survey using number fields or multiple choice so answers are consistent. Review together for bias or confusing wording.

questions.q: Rewrite 'How much screen time do you get?' so answers are consistent.
questions.a: 'On a typical school day, how many hours of recreational screen time do you have? (enter a whole number)' or a multiple-choice range like 0–1, 2–3, 4–5, 6+.

questions.q: Why avoid collecting names in this survey?
questions.a: They aren't needed for the analysis and create privacy risk.

days.guide: Build the survey in Google Forms, send it, collect 15+ responses, and link responses to a spreadsheet.

questions.q: What is metadata in a survey dataset?
questions.a: Data about the data, such as the timestamp of each response or the column descriptions.

days.guide: Clean: standardize entries (e.g. 'yes', 'Yes', 'Y' → 'Yes'), convert text to numbers, remove duplicates, flag impossible values. Have the student document every change.

questions.q: Why is cleaning necessary before analysis?
questions.a: Inconsistent or duplicate entries would be counted wrongly (e.g. 'Yes' and 'yes' as different categories) and produce misleading results.

days.guide: Compare storage options: spreadsheet (easy, small data), database (structured, fast queries, many users), cloud storage (access anywhere, depends on provider and connection).

questions.q: When is a database better than a spreadsheet?
questions.a: When data is large, many users must access or update it at once, or you need fast, complex queries.

days.guide: The student submits the cleaned dataset with a reflection; score with the rubric in the assessment key.

questions.q: Give an example of a cleaning decision that could change a conclusion.
questions.a: Removing an outlier like '20 hours of sleep' raises or lowers the average; deciding to drop incomplete responses could remove a group of people.

weeks.prep: Prepare four small sample datasets (categories, values over time, two numeric variables, one numeric variable). Preview Google Sheets pivot tables (Insert → Pivot table). Pick a public CA data source (e.g. NOAA climate data or EPA AirNow/AirData).
misconceptions: Using a line chart for unrelated categories. Line charts show change over time; bar charts compare categories.
Thinking correlation proves causation. A scatter plot can show two variables move together without one causing the other.
Unlabeled axes or truncated y-axes that exaggerate differences.
weeks.assessment_key: Data story rubric (4 levels): 4 = clear question; an appropriate chart with title, labeled axes and units; a conclusion supported by the chart; at least one limitation (sample size, sampling bias, correlation ≠ causation); answers both follow-up questions accurately; 3 = all parts, limitation vague; 2 = chart or conclusion mismatched to question; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Show bar, line, scatter and histogram charts of the four datasets. Have the student match each to the question it best answers.

questions.q: Which chart shows how a city's temperature changed over a year?
questions.a: Line chart (change over time).

questions.q: Which chart shows whether hours studied relates to test score?
questions.a: Scatter plot (relationship between two numerical variables).

questions.q: Which chart shows how many students fall into each range of sleep hours?
questions.a: Histogram (distribution of one numerical variable).

days.guide: Build a pivot table: rows = a category (e.g. grade level), values = COUNT or AVERAGE of a numeric column. Interpret one row.

questions.q: What does a pivot table do?
questions.a: Summarizes data by grouping rows into categories and calculating counts, sums or averages for each group.

days.guide: The student creates three charts from their survey data, each with a title, labeled axes and a one-sentence takeaway.

questions.q: Your scatter plot shows more screen time with less sleep. Can you say screen time causes less sleep?
questions.a: No — it's a correlation; other factors (age, homework, schedules) could explain both. You'd need an experiment to show cause.

days.guide: Download a CA dataset (daily temperatures or AQI) and make a line chart; identify the trend and any outliers (e.g. AQI spikes during wildfire smoke).

questions.q: What is an outlier?
questions.a: A value far from the rest of the data.

questions.q: What might explain a sudden AQI spike in a California county in late summer?
questions.a: Wildfire smoke.

days.guide: The student presents the 3-slide data story; ask two follow-ups (e.g. 'How could your sample be biased?' 'What would you collect next?'). Score with the rubric.

questions.q: Why should a data story include limitations?
questions.a: So the audience knows how far the conclusion can be trusted and doesn't overgeneralize from limited or biased data.

weeks.prep: Read the Code.org simulations lesson. Plan a 15-minute observation of a store line or drive-through (Day 4) with a stopwatch. Have App Lab open.
misconceptions: Thinking a simulation predicts exactly what will happen. Simulations estimate outcomes based on assumptions and randomness; results vary from run to run.
Expecting exactly 500 heads in 1,000 flips. Results cluster near 50% but vary; larger samples get closer on average.
Forgetting that every model simplifies. Always name what the model leaves out.
weeks.assessment_key: Simulation program checklist: uses randomNumber for arrivals (and/or service time), loops over time steps, tracks queue length and waits, reports average wait; refined version uses the observed arrival rate and a second cashier. Limitations paragraph rubric (4 levels): 4 = names at least two simplifications (e.g. constant service time, no customers leaving, ignores rush hours), explains how refining changed the predicted wait with numbers, and names a decision it could inform (how many cashiers to schedule); 3 = all parts, less specific; 2 = one part missing; 1 = vague.

days.guide: Read the simulations lesson and list three real simulations (weather forecasting, traffic flow, epidemic spread) with what each simplifies (e.g. traffic model treats all drivers alike).

questions.q: Why use a simulation instead of a real experiment?
questions.a: Real experiments may be too costly, dangerous, slow or impossible (e.g. testing an epidemic); simulations let you test many scenarios quickly.

questions.q: What does every simulation do to reality?
questions.a: Simplifies it — it's an abstraction that leaves out details and relies on assumptions.

days.guide: Write a loop that flips a coin 1,000 times: heads += randomNumber(0,1). Display the percentage; run several times and compare to 50%.

questions.q: You get 512 heads out of 1,000. Is the coin unfair?
questions.a: No — 51.2% is normal random variation; results cluster near 50% but are rarely exactly 500.

questions.q: What happens to the percentage if you flip 100,000 times?
questions.a: It tends to get closer to 50% (law of large numbers).

days.guide: Build a checkout simulation: each minute, a customer arrives with some probability (e.g. randomNumber(1,10) <= 3 for 30%); the cashier serves one customer every 3 minutes. Track the line and average wait over 120 minutes.

questions.q: If a customer arrives each minute with probability 0.3, about how many arrive in 60 minutes?

days.guide: Observe a real line for 15 minutes, count arrivals, compute the rate per minute, then update the model. Add a second cashier and compare average waits.

questions.q: You observed 9 arrivals in 15 minutes. What arrival probability per minute should the model use?
Why refine a model with real data?
questions.a: So its assumptions match reality and its predictions are more accurate.

days.guide: The student writes the model-limitations paragraph; score with the rubric in the assessment key.

questions.q: Name one thing the checkout model leaves out.
questions.a: Examples: customers leaving long lines, varying service times, rush-hour arrival changes, self-checkout lanes.

weeks.prep: Open Teachable Machine (teachablemachine.withgoogle.com) and test the image project with a webcam. Choose a credible article on algorithmic bias (e.g. coverage of the 2018 MIT 'Gender Shades' facial-recognition study or the reported Amazon hiring-tool bias). Visit zooniverse.org. Prepare the Unit 6 test.
misconceptions: Thinking computers are neutral so algorithms can't be biased. Algorithms learn from data created by people; biased data or design produces biased results.
Thinking more data always fixes bias. More of the same unrepresentative data repeats the bias; data must be representative.
Believing bias only enters through training data. It can enter in problem definition, data collection, labeling, design choices and how results are used.
weeks.assessment_key: Unit 6 test (12 items): 1) Cleaning = making data consistent and correct. 2) Metadata = data about data. 3) Line chart for change over time. 4) Correlation does not prove causation. 5) Pivot table summarizes by group. 6) Simulation = model of a real process; uses randomness and assumptions. 7) Simulations can be refined using real data. 8) Sampling bias = sample not representative of the population. 9) An online poll about internet access is biased because it excludes people without internet. 10) Training data = examples a machine-learning model learns from. 11) Unbalanced training data makes a model less accurate for underrepresented groups. 12) Crowdsourcing = obtaining input/data from many people online. Mastery 10+/12. Bias checklist (proficient) includes: test with diverse users and data; check training data represents all user groups; measure accuracy separately for each group; examine who could be harmed; get outside review; allow users to report problems.

days.guide: Present five survey scenarios and have the student name the bias, e.g. an online-only poll about internet access (excludes people offline), a gym survey about exercise habits (sample already exercises), a landline phone poll (misses younger people). Rewrite one.

questions.q: Why is an online-only poll about home internet access biased?
questions.a: Only people with internet access can answer, so it overestimates access.

questions.q: How would you fix it?
questions.a: Sample randomly from the whole population using several methods (mail, phone, in person), not just online.

days.guide: In Teachable Machine, train two classes (e.g. 'thumbs up' vs. 'thumbs down') with 50 images of one and 5 of the other, under one lighting condition. Test, then retrain with balanced, varied data and compare accuracy.

questions.q: What happened to accuracy for the class with only 5 examples?
questions.a: It was lower — the model had too few examples to learn that class, so it often predicted the larger class.

questions.q: What is training data?
questions.a: The labeled examples a machine-learning model uses to learn patterns.

days.guide: Read the article and have the student identify where bias entered the pipeline (data collection, labeling, model design, deployment).

questions.q: In the Gender Shades study, what did researchers find about commercial facial-analysis systems?
questions.a: They were much less accurate for darker-skinned women than for lighter-skinned men, largely because training and benchmark data underrepresented darker-skinned faces.

questions.q: Where did bias enter in a hiring algorithm trained on past hires from a male-dominated field?
questions.a: In the training data — it learned patterns from historically biased hiring decisions and penalized résumés associated with women.

days.guide: Explore a Zooniverse project and discuss crowdsourcing/citizen science. Then the student writes a bias-testing checklist for developers.

questions.q: What is citizen science?
questions.a: Scientific research in which members of the public help collect or analyze data, often online.

questions.q: Name one benefit and one risk of crowdsourcing data.
questions.a: Benefit: many people can process huge amounts of data quickly. Risk: contributors may not represent everyone, or quality may vary.

days.guide: Give the Unit 6 test in the assessment key.

questions.q: Give one step to reduce bias in a machine-learning app.
questions.a: Collect training data that represents all user groups, and test accuracy separately for each group before release.

weeks.prep: Preview the student's browser privacy settings and a tracker visualizer (e.g. the browser's built-in privacy report or a tracker-blocker extension). Read the California AG's CCPA overview (oag.ca.gov/privacy/ccpa).
misconceptions: 'I have nothing to hide.' Privacy protects against identity theft, discrimination, manipulation and stalking, not just hiding wrongdoing.
Thinking deleting a post removes it everywhere. Copies, screenshots and backups may remain.
Thinking a single harmless data point is safe. Combining many pieces of PII (birthdate + ZIP + gender) can identify a person.
weeks.assessment_key: Privacy argument essay rubric (4 levels, ~400 words): 4 = clear claim; at least two pieces of evidence from the week (tracker counts, privacy policy findings, CCPA rights, real tradeoffs); addresses a counterargument; explains both safety benefits (finding a lost child, emergency location) and privacy costs (data sold, stalking, breaches); 3 = claim and evidence, weak counterargument; 2 = opinion with little evidence; 1 = off-topic.

days.guide: The student lists PII they've shared (name, birthdate, address, school, photos, location, phone) and rates each risk low/medium/high with a reason.

questions.q: What is PII?
questions.a: Personally identifiable information — data that can identify a specific person, such as name, address, phone number, birthdate, Social Security number or biometric data.

questions.q: Why is birthdate + ZIP code + gender risky together?
questions.a: Combined, they can uniquely identify most people, even without a name.

days.guide: Inspect cookies (browser settings → site data) and site permissions; use a tracker visualizer on a news site and count third-party trackers.

questions.q: What's the difference between a first-party and a third-party cookie?
questions.a: First-party cookies come from the site you're visiting (e.g. keeping you logged in); third-party cookies come from other domains, often advertisers, and can track you across sites.

days.guide: Read a privacy policy for an app the student uses and summarize: data collected, who it's shared with, how to delete it.

questions.q: What three things should you look for in a privacy policy?
questions.a: What data is collected, who it's shared with or sold to, and how you can access or delete it.

days.guide: Learn CCPA/CPRA rights (right to know, delete, correct, opt out of sale/sharing, limit use of sensitive data, non-discrimination). Draft a deletion request email.

questions.q: Name three rights the CCPA/CPRA gives California residents.
questions.a: The right to know what personal information is collected, the right to delete it, and the right to opt out of its sale or sharing (also: correct it, limit sensitive data, non-discrimination).

days.guide: The student writes the 400-word argument; score with the rubric.

questions.q: Give one benefit and one cost of location tracking for safety.
questions.a: Benefit: family or emergency services can find someone in danger. Cost: location history can be leaked, sold or misused for stalking.

weeks.prep: Open the Code.org Caesar cipher, frequency analysis and Vigenère widgets (Unit 'Cybersecurity' lessons). Prepare an encrypted message for the student to crack. Watch a 'public key cryptography paint mixing' explainer (Diffie–Hellman analogy).
misconceptions: Thinking encryption hides that a message exists. It hides the content; others can still see that a message was sent.
Believing a public key must be kept secret. The public key is shared openly; only the private key is secret.

Thinking strong encryption is unbreakable in principle. It's secure because breaking it requires solving a computationally hard problem (e.g. factoring huge numbers) that would take an unreasonable amount of time.
weeks.assessment_key: Cryptography quiz: 1) Encrypt 'CAT' with Caesar shift 3 → 'FDW'. 2) Decrypt 'KHOOR' with shift 3 → 'HELLO'. 3) A Caesar cipher has only 25 useful shifts, so it can be cracked by trying them all (brute force). 4) Frequency analysis works because letters like E, T, A appear most often in English. 5) Vigenère: 'HI' with key 'BB' → 'IJ'. 6) Symmetric encryption = same key encrypts and decrypts. 7) Asymmetric (public key) = public key encrypts, matching private key decrypts. 8) HTTPS uses public-key encryption to securely agree on a shared session key, then symmetric encryption for the data. 9) Public-key encryption relies on problems that are easy to do but very hard to undo (e.g. multiplying two large primes is easy; factoring the product is hard). 10) Key length matters because each added bit doubles the number of possible keys. Score 8+ mastery.

days.guide: Encrypt a sentence with a shift (e.g. 3: A→D). Exchange with a partner and crack theirs using the widget by trying all 25 shifts until English appears.

questions.q: Encrypt 'DOG' with a Caesar shift of 4.
questions.a: HSK.

questions.q: Why is a Caesar cipher easy to crack?
questions.a: There are only 25 possible shifts, so you can try every one (brute force) in seconds.

days.guide: Use the frequency-analysis widget on a random-substitution cipher: match the most common cipher letters to E, T, A, O and look for short words like 'the' and 'a'.

questions.q: A random substitution cipher has 26! possible keys. Why can it still be cracked?
questions.a: Letter frequencies stay the same after substitution, so the most common cipher letters likely stand for E, T, A, etc. — the pattern leaks information.

questions.q: What is the most common letter in English text?
questions.a: E.

days.guide: Teach Vigenère: write the keyword repeated over the message; shift each letter by the key letter's value (A = 0, B = 1 …). Encrypt with a keyword and discuss why longer keys are harder.

questions.q: Encrypt 'CAT' with key 'BAD' (B=1, A=0, D=3).
Why is a longer Vigenère key harder to crack?
questions.a: The pattern repeats less often, so frequency analysis has less repeated structure to work with; a random key as long as the message (a one-time pad) is unbreakable.

days.guide: Model public-key exchange with paint mixing: both share a public color, each adds a secret color, they exchange mixes, then each adds their secret color again to get the same final color an eavesdropper can't un-mix. Connect to HTTPS (padlock icon).

questions.q: In public-key encryption, which key do you share and which do you keep?
questions.a: Share the public key; keep the private key secret. Messages encrypted with your public key can only be decrypted with your private key.

questions.q: What does the padlock / HTTPS mean when you load a site?
questions.a: The connection is encrypted (using TLS), so data between your browser and the site can't be read in transit, and the site's certificate was verified.

days.guide: Give the cryptography quiz in the assessment key.

questions.q: What is the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption?
questions.a: Symmetric uses one shared key to encrypt and decrypt; asymmetric uses a public key to encrypt and a different private key to decrypt.

weeks.prep: Collect 10 sample emails/texts (mix of legitimate and phishing; screenshots from phishing-awareness quizzes work well). Decide which account the student will turn MFA on for (with parent permission).
misconceptions: Thinking phishing is always obvious with bad spelling. Modern phishing can look professional; check sender address, link destination and urgency.
Believing antivirus makes you fully safe. Each measure has limits; layered defenses (updates, backups, MFA, caution) are needed.
Thinking a long password made of a common phrase is unbreakable. Length helps most when combined with unpredictability; never reuse passwords.
weeks.assessment_key: Family cybersecurity guide rubric (4 levels): 4 = five specific actions with reasons tied to real threats, e.g. 1) turn on multifactor authentication (stolen passwords alone won't work), 2) use a password manager with unique long passwords (one breach doesn't unlock other accounts), 3) install software updates promptly (patch known vulnerabilities), 4) back up files offline/in the cloud (recover from ransomware), 5) verify before clicking links or sending money (stop phishing); written clearly for family members; 3 = five actions, some reasons vague; 2 = fewer than five or generic; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Research phishing, malware, ransomware and DDoS and make a chart: how it works, real example (e.g. WannaCry ransomware 2017; Mirai botnet DDoS on Dyn DNS 2016).

questions.q: What does ransomware do?
questions.a: Encrypts the victim's files and demands payment for the key to decrypt them.

questions.q: What is a DDoS attack?
questions.a: A distributed denial-of-service attack floods a server with traffic from many compromised devices so legitimate users can't reach it.

days.guide: The student labels 10 messages as legitimate or phishing and lists clues (mismatched sender domain, urgent threats, links that point elsewhere when hovered, requests for passwords or payment).

questions.q: Name three clues a message is phishing.
questions.a: Sender address doesn't match the real company domain, urgent or threatening language, links whose real URL (on hover) goes somewhere else, and requests for passwords or payment info.

days.guide: Calculate password possibilities using 94 printable characters: 94^8 ≈ 6.1 × 10^15; 94^16 ≈ 3.7 × 10^31. Then turn on MFA for one account.

questions.q: How many 8-character passwords are possible with 94 characters? How many times more for 16?
What is multifactor authentication?
questions.a: Logging in requires two or more kinds of evidence — something you know (password), have (phone/code/key), or are (fingerprint).

days.guide: Match firewalls, antivirus, encryption, updates and backups to threats and note one limit of each.

questions.q: Which measure best protects against losing files to ransomware?
questions.a: Regular backups stored separately (offline or versioned cloud) — you can restore files without paying.

questions.q: What is one limit of a firewall?
questions.a: It filters network traffic but can't stop you from running malware you download or giving your password to a phishing site.

days.guide: The student writes the one-page family cybersecurity guide; score with the rubric.

questions.q: Why are software updates a security measure?
questions.a: Updates patch known vulnerabilities attackers could exploit.

weeks.prep: Help the student choose an innovation and find credible sources (major news outlets, government reports, academic or Pew Research). Prepare the Unit 7 test.
misconceptions: Treating all effects as intended. Many important effects are unintended (e.g. ride-sharing increasing traffic congestion).
Using opinion blogs as evidence. Check author, publisher, date and evidence for credibility.
Thinking an innovation is purely good or purely bad. Most have both beneficial and harmful effects for different groups.
weeks.assessment_key: Unit 7 test (12 items): 1) PII definition. 2) Third-party cookies track across sites. 3) CCPA right to delete. 4) Caesar 'BAD' shift 1 → 'CBE'. 5) Frequency analysis cracks substitution ciphers. 6) Public key shared/private key secret. 7) Phishing = tricking users into revealing info. 8) Ransomware encrypts files for payment. 9) MFA requires multiple factors. 10) DDoS floods a server. 11) Example beneficial and harmful effect of an innovation. 12) Unintended consequence = an outcome not planned by the creators. Mastery 10+/12. Impact essay rubric (4 levels, ~600 words): 4 = clear position on use/regulation, at least three credible cited sources, discusses data the innovation uses, benefits and harms to specific groups, intended and unintended effects, addresses a counterargument; 3 = all elements, less depth; 2 = few sources or one-sided; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: The student chooses an innovation and writes three research questions (What data does it use? Who benefits? Who is harmed?).

questions.q: What makes something a 'computing innovation'?
questions.a: An innovation that includes a program as an integral part of its function (e.g. a self-driving car, a social media app, facial recognition).

days.guide: Find three credible sources and record evidence in a notes table with citations.

questions.q: Name two checks for whether a source is credible.
questions.a: Who wrote/published it and their expertise, whether it cites evidence, and how recent it is (plus checking other sources agree).

days.guide: Build a table of effects: intended vs. unintended and beneficial vs. harmful across social, economic and cultural life.

questions.q: Give an unintended effect of ride-sharing apps.
questions.a: Studies have found they added to traffic congestion in some cities and reduced transit ridership — not what the companies intended.

days.guide: Write the 600-word essay with citations taking a position on use or regulation.

questions.q: What is the difference between a beneficial-intended and a harmful-unintended effect?
questions.a: Beneficial-intended is a planned positive outcome (e.g. faster rides); harmful-unintended is a negative outcome nobody planned (e.g. lost income for taxi drivers).

days.guide: Give the Unit 7 test in the assessment key.

questions.q: Why might generative AI raise both economic benefits and harms?
questions.a: It can make work faster and cheaper (benefit) but may displace some jobs, spread misinformation, or use copyrighted data without permission (harms).

weeks.prep: Create a Trinket (trinket.io) or Replit account. Prepare a short Python program with three syntax errors (missing colon, missing quote, bad indentation). Have the App Lab pet-quiz code open for comparison.
misconceptions: Forgetting that input() returns a string. Use int() or float() before doing math.
Inconsistent indentation. Python uses indentation, not braces, to group code blocks.
Using = in a condition. Python comparisons use ==.
weeks.assessment_key: Python practice set solutions: 1) Even/odd: n = int(input()); print("even" if n % 2 == 0 else "odd"). 2) FizzBuzz: for i in range(1, 101): if i % 15 == 0: print("FizzBuzz") elif i % 3 == 0: print("Fizz") elif i % 5 == 0: print("Buzz") else: print(i) (multiple of 15 must be checked first). 3) Sum to n: total = 0; for i in range(1, n + 1): total += i (n = 10 → 55). 4) Grade letter: if s >= 90 'A' elif s >= 80 'B' elif s >= 70 'C' elif s >= 60 'D' else 'F'. 5) Countdown: for i in range(10, 0, -1): print(i) then print("Liftoff!"). Each program correct on 3 tests = 1 point; 5/5 mastery.

days.guide: Run print("Hello, world!"). Then fix three syntax errors in the provided program, reading the error messages for line numbers.

questions.q: Fix: print("Hi)
questions.a: Add the closing quote: print("Hi").

questions.q: What error do you get from 'if x > 3' with no colon?
questions.a: A SyntaxError — Python requires a colon at the end of an if line.

days.guide: Write a tip calculator: bill = float(input("Bill: ")); tip = bill * 0.18; print(f"Tip: ${tip:.2f}").

questions.q: Why use float() around input()?
questions.a: input() returns a string; float() converts it to a number so you can multiply.

questions.q: What does f"{42.567:.2f}" display?

days.guide: Rewrite the App Lab pet-quiz logic in Python with if/elif/else; place the two versions side by side and list differences (no braces, elif, and/or keywords, colons, indentation).

questions.q: Translate if (a > 5 && b < 3) { … } to Python.
questions.a: if a > 5 and b < 3:  (then an indented block).

questions.q: What is Python's version of JavaScript's 'else if'?
questions.a: elif.

days.guide: Write a number guessing game with while and random.randint(1, 100); write a times table with for i in range(1, 13).

questions.q: What values does range(1, 5) produce?
questions.a: 1, 2, 3, 4 (the end value is excluded).

questions.q: Write a for loop printing the 7 times table up to 7 × 12.
questions.a: for i in range(1, 13): print(7, "x", i, "=", 7 * i)

days.guide: The student solves the five problems in the assessment key; test each with three inputs.

questions.q: What does 17 % 5 give in Python?

weeks.prep: Find the CS50x lecture for the Python week (cs50.harvard.edu/x) and choose a 20–30 minute segment on functions and lists. Ensure Trinket/Replit supports multiple files for the module.
misconceptions: Python lists are 0-indexed and slicing excludes the end index: scores[1:3] gives items at index 1 and 2.
Printing inside a function instead of returning, so the result can't be reused.
Forgetting to import the module (import mymodule) or calling functions without the module prefix.
weeks.assessment_key: Mini-project rubric (4 levels): 4 = uses a list, a loop and at least two well-named functions with parameters/return values stored in a separate module that is imported; runs correctly on test inputs; student clearly explains how the functions decompose the problem; 3 = works, explanation weak or functions in the same file; 2 = missing list, loop or functions; 1 = doesn't run.

days.guide: Create scores = [88, 92, 75, 100]; practice append, len, and slicing; traverse to find max and average without built-ins, then compare with max() and sum()/len().

questions.q: For scores = [88, 92, 75, 100], what is the average?
What is scores[1:3]?

days.guide: Write to_fahrenheit(c) and is_vowel(ch) with def and return; test each with three inputs.

questions.q: What does to_fahrenheit(37) return using c * 9/5 + 32?
questions.a: 98.6 (Python may show 98.60000000000001 due to round-off).

questions.q: Write is_vowel.
questions.a: def is_vowel(ch): return ch.lower() in "aeiou"

days.guide: Watch the CS50 segment; the student notes two ideas that match App Lab (e.g. functions = procedures with parameters; lists and loops = traversal).

questions.q: Name one way Python functions are like App Lab functions.
questions.a: Both take parameters, can return values, and let you name and reuse a block of code (procedural abstraction).

days.guide: Build the mini project with functions in a separate module (e.g. grades.py) imported into main.py.

questions.q: Why put functions in a separate module?
questions.a: It organizes code, lets the functions be reused in other programs, and keeps the main program short and readable.

days.guide: The student demos the project and explains the decomposition; score with the rubric.

questions.q: How does decomposition help a larger program?
questions.a: Each function handles one subproblem, so it can be written, tested and fixed independently.

weeks.prep: Read the current AP CSP Create performance task requirements and scoring guidelines (AP Central / AP Students site), since the exact format can change year to year. Print the checklist.
misconceptions: Choosing a project too big to finish. Favor a simple program that clearly uses a list and a procedure.
Using a list that isn't necessary (e.g. storing one value). The list must manage complexity — the program would be harder to write without it.
Writing a procedure without a parameter that affects its behavior, or without sequencing, selection and iteration.
weeks.assessment_key: Plan checklist review — the plan passes when it includes: [ ] program purpose and intended user; [ ] input from the user (or other source); [ ] a list that stores data and is used to fulfill the purpose; [ ] a student-developed procedure with at least one parameter that affects its functionality; [ ] an algorithm inside the procedure that includes sequencing, selection and iteration; [ ] a call to the procedure; [ ] output based on input and program functionality; [ ] UI sketch with user feedback noted. Missing items must be revised before Week 34.

days.guide: Read the Create task requirements together and build the checklist from them.

questions.q: What must the student-developed procedure include?
questions.a: At least one parameter that affects its functionality, and an algorithm that includes sequencing, selection and iteration.

days.guide: Brainstorm five program ideas for a real user; score each on purpose, feasibility and how naturally it uses a list (e.g. quiz app with a list of questions, workout planner, recipe filter).

questions.q: Why is a 'quiz app with a list of questions' a good fit?
questions.a: The list naturally stores many questions, and a procedure can loop through it and check answers with conditionals.

days.guide: Write the plan: purpose, the list and what it manages, the procedure in pseudocode.

questions.q: How would your program be different without the list?
questions.a: A strong answer: it would need many separate variables and repeated code, and couldn't easily grow — showing the list manages complexity.

days.guide: Sketch UI screens and walk a user through them; record feedback.

questions.q: What feedback is most useful at this stage?
questions.a: Where the user is confused about what to do next or what the output means.

days.guide: Review the plan against the checklist in the assessment key; revise missing items.

questions.q: Which three programming constructs must appear in the procedure's algorithm?
questions.a: Sequencing, selection (if) and iteration (loop).

weeks.prep: Set up a development log (date, what was done, problems, next steps). Arrange a peer reviewer (co-op, online CS community or local programming club) and a shared doc for feedback.
misconceptions: Coding everything before testing. Develop incrementally: add one feature, test, then add the next.
Testing only 'happy path' inputs. Include edge cases: empty input, very large numbers, no matches.

Getting too much help from others on the code. The College Board requires the program's code and written work be the student's own; collaborators' or AI help must follow current AP rules and be acknowledged.
weeks.assessment_key: Development log rubric: 4 = dated entries every day describing progress, bugs and fixes; screens, list and procedure all working; at least four test cases (including two edge cases) with expected vs. actual and fixes; peer feedback recorded with a response; 3 = all parts, fewer details; 2 = missing tests or log entries; 1 = incomplete. Sample proficient test case: input = empty text box; expected = 'Please enter a value'; actual = crashed → fixed by adding a check.

days.guide: Build screens and event handlers; log progress.

questions.q: What's the difference between iterative and incremental development?
questions.a: Iterative: repeatedly refining the whole program through cycles of feedback and testing. Incremental: building it in small working pieces, adding one feature at a time.

days.guide: Code the list and display it to verify it's populated correctly.

questions.q: How can you check your list is populated correctly?
questions.a: Display or console.log the list and its length and compare to the expected data.

days.guide: Write the procedure with a parameter, using sequencing, selection and iteration; call it from an event.

questions.q: Point to the selection and iteration in your procedure.
questions.a: Answers vary; e.g. the FOR EACH loop through the list (iteration) and the IF that checks each item against the parameter (selection).

days.guide: Write and run at least four test cases, including edge cases; record expected vs. actual.

questions.q: Give an edge case for a program that filters a list by a user's choice.
questions.a: A choice that matches no items, or matches every item; also empty input.

days.guide: Share the program with a peer; give and receive feedback in a shared document.

questions.q: How should you respond to peer feedback?
questions.a: Record it, decide which suggestions improve the program for users, and note what you changed and why.

weeks.prep: Install or locate a screen recorder (built into Windows: Xbox Game Bar Win+G; Mac: Shift-Cmd-5; or a browser tool). Re-read the current Create task video and Personalized Project Reference (PPR) requirements on the College Board site.
misconceptions: Video too long or with voice narration. The video must be 1 minute or less and must not contain voice narration (captions are allowed) and must not show personally identifying information.
Including comments in the PPR code segments. The PPR code segments must not include comments.
Forgetting to acknowledge others' code or media. Any code or media from others must be cited in code comments.
weeks.assessment_key: Create task self-score (current College Board rubric): check each row — program purpose and function demonstrated in the video (input, functionality, output); data abstraction (list stores data and is used); managing complexity (list makes the program simpler); procedural abstraction (procedure with parameter, called); algorithm implementation (sequencing, selection and iteration in the procedure); testing (two calls with different arguments producing different results). Proficient submission: video ≤ 1 minute, no narration, no PII; PPR includes list creation, list use, procedure definition and a call, no comments; written-response practice answers name exactly how the list and procedure work.

days.guide: Two users test the program; note usability and accessibility problems (text size, contrast, unclear instructions); prioritize fixes.

questions.q: Name one accessibility improvement for an app.
questions.a: Larger text and high color contrast, clear labels on buttons, not relying on color alone, alt text for images.

days.guide: Fix top issues, add code comments, and add acknowledgments with license attribution for any outside code or media.

questions.q: How should you acknowledge an image you used from another source?
questions.a: In a code comment: the source/author, URL and license (e.g. 'Image: "Cat" by J. Doe, CC BY 2.0, via Openverse').

days.guide: Record a 1-minute-or-less video showing input, functionality and output (no voice, no PII).

questions.q: What must the video show?
questions.a: Input to the program, at least one aspect of the program's functionality, and output produced.

days.guide: Capture list and procedure code segments in the PPR (no comments) and practice the written-response prompts.

questions.q: Practice: explain how your program would be written differently without the list.
questions.a: A proficient answer describes the specific data, says it would require separate variables for each item and repeated code, and explains it couldn't handle more items without rewriting.

days.guide: Submit the code, video and PPR (to AP Digital Portfolio if registered) and self-score with the rubric.

questions.q: What does it mean that your procedure's parameter 'affects functionality'?
questions.a: Calling the procedure with different arguments produces different behavior or results.

weeks.prep: Use Khan Academy AP CSP unit tests and College Board released/practice questions. Build or obtain a 70-question practice exam (AP Classroom if registered) and a cumulative final (e.g. 40 questions covering the five big ideas).
misconceptions: Rushing pseudocode traces in your head. Write a trace table for every variable.
Missing 'NOT' or 'all of the following EXCEPT' wording. Underline negatives in the question.
Over-studying favorite topics. Use the error analysis to focus on the weakest big idea.
weeks.assessment_key: Practice exam: score with the answer key that accompanies the source (AP scaled scores roughly track 60–70%+ correct for a 4–5). Final exam representative items and answers: 1) 10011₂ = 19. 2) 2^7 = 128 patterns from 7 bits. 3) Overflow vs. round-off examples. 4) Lossless for text, lossy for streaming. 5) DNS maps names to IPs. 6) Fault tolerance through redundancy. 7) L ← [2, 5, 8]; APPEND(L, 1); L[4] → 1. 8) x ← 3; REPEAT 3 TIMES { x ← x * 2 } → 24. 9) Binary search requires sorted list; 1,000 items → at most 10 checks. 10) 2ⁿ is unreasonable time. 11) Public-key: share public, keep private. 12) Phishing defense: check sender and links. 13) Bias from unrepresentative training data. 14) Citizen science / crowdsourcing definition. 15) Copyright vs. Creative Commons. Mastery 80%+. Reflection: full credit for specific growth examples (a bug they learned to fix, a concept that clicked).

days.guide: Do Khan Academy practice on binary, compression, the internet and fault tolerance; correct every error.

questions.q: Why can't lossy compression be reversed?
questions.a: It permanently removes data, so the original can't be reconstructed.

days.guide: Trace 20 AP pseudocode problems on lists, loops, procedures and Boolean logic.

questions.q: L ← [3, 6, 9]; total ← 0; FOR EACH n IN L { IF n > 4 { total ← total + n } }. Final total?

days.guide: Give the timed 70-question practice exam (120 minutes) under test conditions.

questions.q: How many minutes per question does 120 minutes for 70 questions allow?
questions.a: About 1.7 minutes (≈ 1 minute 43 seconds) per question.

days.guide: Categorize missed questions by big idea (Creative Development, Data, Algorithms and Programming, Computer Systems and Networks, Impact of Computing) and redo each with an explanation.

questions.q: Name the five AP CSP big ideas.
questions.a: Creative Development, Data, Algorithms and Programming, Computer Systems and Networks, Impact of Computing.

days.guide: Give the cumulative final and have the student write a short reflection on growth as a programmer.

questions.q: x ← 3; REPEAT 3 TIMES { x ← x * 2 }. Final x?
